scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

First, the situation: The dad noticed that more money was missing than usual. He planted a $20 bill to catch his daughter, who took it. He then called the police, took her out of class, and the officers found out that she was being bullied and had to buy lunch for herself and a friend. The daughter was silent on the way home, and when they got home, the mom was upset, thinking this approach would damage their relationship with their daughter. The daughter apologized but said she didn't want her parents to intervene because she was scared of retaliation from the bully and losing her friend. So, the dad's intention was to teach his daughter a lesson about stealing. He thought that involving the police would make her understand the seriousness of the action. But the outcome was that the daughter felt scared, and the mom was angry, thinking this was a bad approach. I need to consider a few things here. First, was the dad's method appropriate? Involving the police is a strong measure, especially for a child. It might have been more effective to talk to her first, understand why she was taking the money, and address the underlying issues. The fact that she was being bullied and had to buy lunch for a friend shows that there were other problems at school that the dad wasn't aware of. By calling the police, he not only addressed the stealing but also exposed her to potential embarrassment and fear of retaliation. Another point is the emotional impact on the daughter. She was silent on the way home, which suggests she was upset or scared. The mom's reaction was also strong, indicating that this approach might have damaged the family's trust and relationship with their daughter. The daughter felt that she had to steal because she didn't want her parents to intervene, which shows that she was trying to handle the situation on her own but ended up making a mistake. I also think about the effectiveness of the lesson. Teaching a child that stealing is wrong is important, but using the police might have been too harsh. It could have made the daughter feel like she was treated like a criminal, which might not be the best way to teach responsibility. Instead, a more understanding and supportive approach might have been better, where the parents listen to her reasons, help her deal with the bullying, and guide her on how to handle such situations without resorting to stealing. In conclusion, while the dad's intention was to teach a lesson, the method he chose might have been too extreme and counterproductive. It led to emotional distress for the daughter, strained the family relationship, and didn't address the root cause of why she was taking the money. A more empathetic and supportive approach would have been more appropriate in this situation.
